turn_text: First question is, recently you appeared with Governor Romney in Chicago. And in your book, you talk at length about the 2012 election, your vetting process, and some takeaways from the election. In your view, what was the biggest mistake made by the campaign? Well, I try to talk about the notion of a referendum versus a choice, and that strategy. And the typical conventional wisdom in a campaign like that is to make it a referendum on an unpopular incumbent. And my personal experiences have always been to make them sharp choices in contrast. And those two strategies don't have to be mutually exclusive. But I like to have elections where you're running on specifically how you'll do things differently so that when you win, you have the obligation and the mall authority to do it. At the end we close that way. The other, you know, regret is that our party, you know, didn't have time to voter print on technology we needed. You have a lot of, the incumbents have such a competitive advantage. You know, you come out of the primary like Mitt did with no money in May. You don't get your general election money until mid August and the incumbent pounds you for three or four months in the battleground states defining you before you can define yourself. And so there are a lot of competitive disadvantages. Some of those are structural that need to be addressed. But just the way I see where the country is headed, the liberal progressive philosophy that's on display and in practice, the policy that flowed from it, I really believe we need to give the country a really clear choice of what founding principles look like in practice today and how if applied to the moment, can offer solutions and policies that can renew the American idea, get our country back on top, put us on a different track, bring that to the country, make our case, have the elections, and then if you win, and I think we can and will, then do it. And that's the kind of election we need to have. We need to give it to the country before it's too late, because I do worry that we're running against a clock here. And I worry that we can become a social welfare state, like a European, Western social democracy, very quickly, if we don't watch it. And we need to not only criticize and explain why that's an empty promise, but also we have to explain what we would do differently and what kind of world it looks like. And I believe that people really have a great affinity for the American idea, for the founders vision. And I think we need to reinvigorate that. Sure, and to the end in your book, you lay out a very robust agenda with monetary, fiscal, regulatory, all matter of reforms. Yeah, specifically corny capitalism, go after corny capitalism, re-inject sound money, get the regulators back in their constitutional parameters and boxes, allow businesses to grow, allow the economy to thrive and do welfare reform 2.0 so we can work on getting people from welfare to work. and make sure our country is strong and safe by not denoting our military forces and having a foreign policy that is strategic. And to that end, if you were to implement your agenda, would you be slowing the rate of growth of government or would you actually be shrinking from the base line? No, I think you need to shrink from the base line. Look, we've played with these things before. I'm just going to get crewed numbers. For the last 60 years, we have basically taken about 20% of GDP out of the economy for the government. If you just take today's government and keep it on its track where we are, we'll be at 40% of GDP by the time I've got grandkids running around America. And so slowing the rate of growth, does that mean we're supposed to be complicit with 30% of GDP instead of 40% not at all? And so I really think we need to go back to the basics back to reliveting government so that it does what it's supposed to do and it doesn't effectively and then it's held there so that civil society, charity and community and a free market economy can fill the rest of that space for American life. To me, it's a vision of a society-centered vision that's collaborative versus a government-centered vision that is coercive. That is the choice we have going for us And it is not just a more efficient task culture for a welfare state, it is get America back to first principles, get our government re-limited and focused so that we can have a society-centered vision for American life that is collaborative, that is growth-oriented, and that is secure. Right. And one element of that, which you mentioned previously, is chronic capitalism. And you say in your book, Republicans should be staunchly opposed to corporate welfare in any form. and to the codes of relationship between government and big business that undermines the dynamism of our economy. Now, how do you reconcile that for readers who are skeptical and feel betrayed by government and by Republicans in particular?
